# Are the patent's I-shaped ring resonators tuned from the inside or from the edge?

**Research date:** 2026-09-04
**Ticket:** [#138](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/138) — generated by [#130](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/130), part of [#104](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/104).
**Question:** US12089385B2's Example 3 uses I-shaped electric ring resonators. If one were used as a *letter* in a coding-metasurface alphabet, would it be tuned by moving its outer edge — which changes the gap to its neighbour and therefore how strongly the two interfere — or from its interior, which leaves that gap alone?

Every source below is either **retrieved** (downloaded and read in this session) or explicitly marked **STRANDED**. Nothing recalled is presented as checked.

---

## Bottom line up front

**Five findings, in order of how much they change things.**

**1. Example 3 is not an original design. It is Landy et al.'s 2008 "Perfect Metamaterial Absorber", reproduced symbol for symbol and number for number.** The patent's FIG. 7F table reads `a₁ = 4.2, a₂ = 12, t = 0.6, G = 0.6, W = 4, L = 1.7, H = 11.8 mm`. Landy et al.'s fabricated device reads, verbatim, *"a1=4.2, a2=12, W=4, G=0.6, t=0.6, L=1.7, H=11.8"*, on FR4, with the two metal layers *"separated by 0.72mm"* — the patent's `h = 0.72 mm`. Same symbols, same values, same substrate, same spacing, same ERR-over-cut-wire architecture. This is the single most useful thing found in this pass, because it means **the element's own designers state in print how they tune it**, and because **this geometry has been measured** — something [#116](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/116) concluded did not exist anywhere.

**2. The tuning parameter is a choice, not a property — and the two choices sit at opposite ends of the ledger.** The patent never says which dimension moves the resonance. Landy et al. do, for their own design, and their answer is an interior-and-out-of-plane one: they tune the magnetic resonance *"by changing the geometry of the cut wire and the separation between the cut wire and electric resonator"*, explicitly *"without changing the geometry of the electric resonator"*. But an alphabet needs more range than that, and the obvious lever — the cut wire's length `H` — is a perimeter lever on the worst possible axis. The three candidate knobs give **gap-to-neighbour excursions of 1.0× (interior gap `G`), 7.7× (ERR width `W`), and 20.7× (cut-wire length `H`)** for the same 1.5:1 spread in resonant frequency. Costanzo's square patch — the family #130 ruled out — is **21.1×**. So tuning this element by the cut wire reproduces the square patch's problem almost exactly; tuning it by its interior gap removes it entirely.

**3. The preliminary 0.2 mm arithmetic is confirmed exactly — but it is on the wrong plane, and there is a second 0.2 mm nobody had noticed.** `W` = 4 mm inside `a₁` = 4.2 mm does leave **0.2 mm = 0.0067 λ at 10 GHz**, tighter than the tightest gap in Costanzo's range. But `a₁` is the **H-plane** — Landy's Fig. 1(c) puts **E along `a₂`**, and on that axis the resonators are **8.0 mm = 0.267 λ apart**, looser than the *loosest* gap Costanzo reports. The 0.2 mm that lands on the E-plane belongs to the **cut wire on the underside**: `H` = 11.8 mm in `a₂` = 12 mm, also 0.2 mm, also 0.0067 λ. The tight gap is real, but it is on the bottom layer, not the top one the ticket was looking at.

**4. `docs/supercell-sizing-rule.md` does not survive this cell, and the failure is in the alphabet's favour.** The rule's headline — *"N = 2 is usually the only block size allowed, and at N = 2 the block averages nothing"* — is a property of a roughly half-wavelength **square** cell. On a 4.2 × 12 mm cell at 10 GHz, **N = 2 produces no propagating scattered lobe at all**; the smallest usable block is **5 × 2 cells (21 × 24 mm)**, and the coding axis is subject to a hard floor of **a block at least λ/2 across, which is 3.57 cells on the `a₁` axis**. Because blocks of 4–5 cells and up are *forced*, the boundary fraction drops below 1 and **the block does average**. Four amendments are set out in §5.

**5. There is a published, measured, fixed-outline alphabet for this element family, and it is directly actionable.** Withayachumnankul, Fumeaux & Abbott built five ELC resonators sharing **exactly the same 14 mm cell and the same 12 mm outer footprint**, differing only in the interior capacitor, and measured resonances from **2.10 to 3.14 GHz — a 1.50× range at literally zero gap excursion**. The trick is to replace the plain capacitive gap with an interdigital capacitor and vary the finger count. Their design law is closed-form, and the finger count is an integer, which suits #130's "admit only the quantised set" exactly.

**The one-line answer.** The I-shape **passes the interior-tuning test if, and only if, the alphabet is built on the interior gap rather than on the cut wire or the outer width** — and unlike the square patch, it genuinely has that option, with a measured precedent. What it does *not* buy is immunity: a control experiment on the same element family, with geometry held perfectly identical and only the electrical tuning changed, still measured **6.9% of unlike-neighbour frequency pulling** (§4.3). Interior tuning removes the capacitive mechanism, not the inductive one.

---

## 1. What the element actually is

### 1.1 The shape, read off the drawings

The patent's FIG. 7E was rendered from the [Google Patents PDF](https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/f5/d9/73/7d2e4472adfcb1/US12089385.pdf) at up to 2400 dpi and the halftone averaged out numerically, because the scan has no text layer. The topology is:

- A **rectangular metal frame**: a top bar and a bottom bar, each running the full width `W`, joined at the left and right by side arms.
- A **central vertical post of width `t` = 0.6 mm** bridging the top and bottom bars.
- **Two gaps `G` = 0.6 mm**, one cutting through the *left* arm and one through the *right* arm, both at mid-height.

Read as a conductor, the continuous part is top bar → central post → bottom bar: a capital **I** with serifs. Hence the patent's name. The four stubs hanging off the ends of the bars form the two capacitor plates across the `G` gaps.

In plain terms: **it is a metal picture-frame with a bar down the middle and a small break cut into each side.** Electrically it is a loop (an inductor) closed by two small breaks (capacitors) — an LC circuit whose resonant frequency is set by the loop's size and the breaks' size.

### 1.2 The same shape, from a much better drawing

Searching for the element family turned up **Landy, Sajuyigbe, Mock, Smith & Padilla, "A Perfect Metamaterial Absorber", [arXiv:0803.1670](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.1670)**, published as *Phys. Rev. Lett.* **100**, 207402 (2008). Retrieved in full. Its Fig. 1 is the patent's FIG. 7E, in colour, with the same six symbols in the same places, plus a field-orientation axis triad the patent omits.

The numbers are identical. Landy et al. give two sets — the ideal simulated one and the one they could actually etch:

> "the metamaterial had the dimensions, in millimeters, of: a1=4.2, a2=12, W=3.9, G=0.606, t=0.6, L=1.7, H=11.8, and the metamaterials elements were separated by 0.65 in the ẑ direction."
>
> "we fabricated a metamaterial which deviated slightly from the ideal absorber and had the dimensions, in millimeters, of: a1=4.2, a2=12, W=4, G=0.6, t=0.6, L=1.7, H=11.8."
>
> "The end results was that the metamaterials elements were separated by 0.72mm in the ẑ direction."

The patent's FIG. 7F table is the **fabricated** set, plus `h = 0.72 mm`. Both are on FR4.

Measuring Landy's Fig. 1 directly (colour separation of the metal against the cell outline) confirms it is drawn exactly to scale: the cell measures 155 × 443 px against `a₁`/`a₂` = 4.2/12 mm, giving **36.90 and 36.92 px/mm on the two axes** — agreement to 0.05%. Against that scale the ERR's metal bounding box is **146 × 146 px = 3.96 × 3.96 mm**, i.e. **square, W × W ≈ 4 × 4 mm**, and exactly centred in the cell. The patent's own FIG. 7E gives the same to the precision its halftone allows (≈3.8–4.0 mm). **The ERR's height is not in either dimension table**; it has to be measured, and this is where it comes from.

### 1.3 Which way the fields point — and why it matters

Landy's Fig. 1(c) carries the axis triad the patent lacks: **E ∥ x̂, H ∥ ŷ, k ∥ ẑ**, with x̂ along the long (`a₂`) axis of the cell. The paper's boundary conditions confirm it independently — *"perfect electric (ŷẑ-plane) and perfect magnetic (x̂ẑ-plane)"*, which forces E perpendicular to the PEC walls, i.e. along x̂.

So: **E lies along `a₂` = 12 mm. H lies along `a₁` = 4.2 mm.**

This matters because Costanzo's protocol deliberately swaps the **E-plane** neighbours, *"as they give higher mutual coupling levels and consequently higher phase errors with respect to the H plane case"* (`docs/local-periodicity-coupling-error.md` §2.1). The ticket's preliminary observation put the 0.2 mm gap on the axis it assumed was the sensitive one. It is on the other one.

### 1.4 The geometry, laid out

At 10 GHz, λ₀ = 29.979 mm. **CALCULATED** from the FIG. 7F table plus the ERR height measured in §1.2.

| Layer | Element | Along `a₁` = 4.2 mm (**H-plane**) | Along `a₂` = 12 mm (**E-plane**) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | I-shaped ERR, 4.0 × 4.0 mm | gap **0.2 mm = 0.0067 λ** | gap **8.0 mm = 0.267 λ** |
| Bottom | cut wire, 1.7 × 11.8 mm | gap 2.5 mm = 0.083 λ | gap **0.2 mm = 0.0067 λ** |
| — | cell pitch | 0.140 λ | 0.400 λ |

Two readings worth stating plainly.

**The ticket's arithmetic is confirmed.** 4.2 − 4 = 0.2 mm; 0.2/29.979 = 0.00667 λ. Costanzo's square-patch alphabet at 0.4 λ pitch runs from 0.009 λ to 0.19 λ, so 0.0067 λ is indeed **tighter than his tightest, before any tuning at all**. At 0.2 mm the top layer is barely an array of separate resonators: it is closer to one continuous ladder-shaped conductor with a small break every 4.2 mm, and that break is *part of the resonator*, not a nuisance.

**But the tight gap is on the weak-coupling plane, and there is a second one on the strong plane.** The E-plane ERR-to-ERR gap is 8.0 mm — *looser* than Costanzo's loosest. Meanwhile the **cut wire**, on the underside, sits 0.2 mm from its E-plane neighbour. Whether the tight H-plane gap on the top layer or the tight E-plane gap on the bottom layer dominates is **not settled by anything retrieved in this pass** and is the single most important thing a solve would answer (§7).

## 2. Which dimension is the tuning parameter?

### 2.1 The patent does not say

The description text was searched in full. Everything it offers on tuning Example 3 is one sentence:

> "By combining the two different shapes (i.e., electric ring resonator (ERR) in the top and wire resonator in the bottom), the electric resonance and magnetic resonance can be tuned to overlap each other which results in no reflected signal."

That names *what* is tuned (the two resonances, into coincidence) and not *which dimension does it*. It also confirms Example 3's architecture is the classical two-resonator absorber: one element that responds to the electric field, a second that responds to the magnetic field, arranged so both resonate at the same frequency, at which point the surface neither reflects nor transmits.

The patent's own reference list points at ELC and SRR variants (Gu et al., *JAP* **108**:064913; Ghosh et al., *JAP* **115**:104503; Singh et al., *APL* **99**:264101) but does not cite Landy et al.

### 2.2 What the element's designers say

Landy et al. state their tuning strategy twice, and it is an interior/out-of-plane strategy:

> "We used this design instead of a conventional split-wire design because of the limitations of straight wire media, i.e. a split-wire design has **limited tunability** beyond the addition of more wires per unit cell to increase inductance."

> "We were then able to tune the magnetic response by **changing the geometry of the cut wire and the separation between the cut wire and electric resonator**. By manipulating the magnetic coupling **without changing the geometry of the electric resonator**, we able to decouple ε and µ, and therefore individually tune each resonance."

Two things follow.

**They chose the ERR precisely because a plain cut wire has too little tuning range.** That is a designer's judgement about *this family*, in print, and it says the ERR's virtue is that its resonance can be moved by something other than making it bigger.

**Their stated knobs are the cut wire and the dielectric spacing `h`** — the second is out of plane and touches no gap at all, which is exactly the lever [#104](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/104) already records ("sweep the dielectric spacing instead, which is what actually moves a resonance"). But `h` is a *stack* variable: every letter in an alphabet shares one substrate, so it cannot vary letter to letter on a single printed surface. It tunes the design, not the alphabet.

### 2.3 The general law, and how strong each lever is

Both the ELC papers retrieved state the same framework: the resonator is a loop (inductance `L`) closed by a gap (capacitance `C`), and **f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))**. Withayachumnankul et al. write it as `f₀ = 1/(π√(2LC))` for their series arrangement; the scaling is what matters. Their statement of the levers:

> "these approaches are based on the idea of raising the overall inductance and capacitance… A straightforward way is to change the feature sizes of the structure, i.e., **shorten gaps** or **lengthen wires** to increase the capacitance and inductance, respectively. However, the realization of this simple approach can be limited by fabrication tolerances."

"Shorten gaps" is interior. "Lengthen wires" is perimeter. Both work; they are not equally strong, and they are not equally safe.

**How weak is the interior gap on its own?** Withayachumnankul et al.'s Eq. (3) gives the coplanar gap capacitance as `C₀ ∝ (K(k)/K′(k))·l₀` with `k = tan²[0.25wπ/(w+g)]` — a ratio of elliptic integrals, which varies roughly logarithmically with the gap `g`, not as 1/`g`. Evaluating it at Example 3's own conductor width `w` = `t` = 0.6 mm (**CALCULATED** from their formula):

| `G` (mm) | 0.15 | 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.4 | **0.6** | 0.9 | 1.2 | 1.8 | 2.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C relative to `G` = 0.6 | 1.61 | 1.47 | 1.28 | 1.16 | **1.00** | 0.87 | 0.78 | 0.68 | 0.62 |
| f₀ relative to `G` = 0.6 | 0.79 | 0.83 | 0.88 | 0.93 | **1.00** | 1.07 | 1.13 | 1.21 | 1.27 |

Sweeping `G` across a **16× range (0.15 → 2.4 mm)** — which is roughly all the room there is inside a 4 mm-tall ERR — changes the capacitance by only **2.6×** and the frequency by **1.61×**. That is a real alphabet's worth of range, but it is bought expensively, and the low end runs into the printer's floor.

The comparison that matters is not the size of the swing but *which* capacitance swings. **Sweeping `G` changes the resonator's own capacitance by 2.6× and the neighbour-coupling capacitance by nothing.** Costanzo's square patch changes the neighbour-coupling capacitance by 20×. Those are the two numbers on opposite sides of the ledger.

### 2.4 The knobs, and what each does to the outline

**INFERRED** — from §1 geometry plus §2.3 mechanism. The right-hand column is the whole question #138 was asked.

| Knob | What it is | Layer | Moves the outer bounding box? | Which neighbour gap moves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `G` | the split gap in the side arms | top | **No** | none |
| `t` | central post width | top | **No** | none |
| arm width | (unnamed in the table) | top | **No** | none |
| interdigital fingers `N` | §6's variant | top | **No** | none |
| `W` | ERR outer width | top | **Yes**, along `a₁` | the 0.2 mm **H-plane** gap |
| ERR height | (unnamed; ≈ `W`) | top | **Yes**, along `a₂` | the 8.0 mm E-plane gap |
| `H` | cut-wire length | bottom | **Yes**, along `a₂` | the 0.2 mm **E-plane** gap |
| `L` | cut-wire width | bottom | **Yes**, along `a₁` | the 2.5 mm gap |
| `h` | dielectric spacing | stack | No (out of plane) | none — but cannot vary per letter |

## 3. The gap-to-neighbour excursion, per knob

This is the quantity Costanzo reports as 0.009 λ → 0.19 λ. **CALCULATED**, on one stated assumption: that the tuned dimension sets the resonance as `f₀ ∝ 1/size`, which is the standard first-order scaling for both a loop resonator and a cut-wire dipole. `R` is the ratio between the alphabet's highest and lowest resonant frequency — how far apart the letters have to sit.

| `R` | Knob | Dimension range (mm) | Gap range (mm) | Gap range (λ at 10 GHz) | **Gap ratio** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | `W` (ERR, H-plane) | 3.64 – 4.00 | 0.20 – 0.56 | 0.0067 – 0.019 | 2.8× |
| | `H` (wire, **E-plane**) | 10.73 – 11.80 | 0.20 – 1.27 | 0.0067 – 0.043 | 6.4× |
| | `G` (interior) | outline fixed | 0.20 – 0.20 | 0.0067 | **1.0×** |
| 1.2 | `W` | 3.33 – 4.00 | 0.20 – 0.87 | 0.0067 – 0.029 | 4.3× |
| | `H` | 9.83 – 11.80 | 0.20 – 2.17 | 0.0067 – 0.072 | 10.8× |
| | `G` | outline fixed | 0.20 – 0.20 | 0.0067 | **1.0×** |
| 1.5 | `W` | 2.67 – 4.00 | 0.20 – 1.53 | 0.0067 – 0.051 | 7.7× |
| | `H` | 7.87 – 11.80 | 0.20 – 4.13 | 0.0067 – **0.138** | **20.7×** |
| | `G` | outline fixed | 0.20 – 0.20 | 0.0067 | **1.0×** |
| 2.0 | `W` | 2.00 – 4.00 | 0.20 – 2.20 | 0.0067 – 0.073 | 11.0× |
| | `H` | 5.90 – 11.80 | 0.20 – 6.10 | 0.0067 – 0.204 | 30.5× |
| | `G` | outline fixed | 0.20 – 0.20 | 0.0067 | **1.0×** |
| — | **Costanzo square patch, 0.4 λ** | — | — | **0.009 – 0.19** | **21.1×** |

**The line to read is `H` at `R` = 1.5: 0.0067 λ → 0.138 λ, a 20.7× gap ratio, against the square patch's 21.1×.** Tuning Example 3 by its cut-wire length is not *like* the square patch's problem — arithmetically it is the same problem, on the strong-coupling plane, to within 2%.

Tuning by `W` is roughly three times gentler (7.7× at the same `R`) and sits on the weak-coupling plane, but it is also **one-sided**: `W` is already 95% of `a₁`, so every letter can only be *smaller* than the reference, and the alphabet cannot be centred on Example 3's own geometry.

Tuning by `G` moves nothing. That is the entire point.

## 4. What interior tuning does and does not buy

### 4.1 What it removes

Costanzo's mechanism, quoted in `docs/local-periodicity-coupling-error.md` §2.1: *"the heavy variations in the gap distance between adjacent patches … cause very dissimilar mutual coupling levels that make unreliable periodic boundary conditions."* If the gap does not vary, that sentence does not apply. An interior-tuned alphabet has **zero** gap-distance variation by construction, so the 20× capacitance-variation term is identically absent.

### 4.2 A measured demonstration that it works

**Withayachumnankul, Fumeaux & Abbott, "Compact electric-LC resonators for metamaterials", [arXiv:1009.0139](https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.0139); *Optics Express* **18**(25):25912–25921 (2010).** Retrieved in full.

Five ELC designs, fabricated as 9 × 9 arrays on 0.8 mm FR4 and measured between horns:

> "the five designs share the unit cell size a, gap width g, and cross-sectional length of the loaded capacitor. … the structural parameters common to all designs are w = g = 0.4 mm, b = 0.8 mm, d = 12 mm, and a = 14 mm."

`d` = 12 mm is the resonator's outer footprint; `a` = 14 mm is the cell. **Every letter therefore presents exactly the same 2 mm gap to its neighbour.** What differs is only the capacitor inside: a plain gap in the reference, an interdigital capacitor with `N` fingers of length `l_IDC` in the other four.

| Sample | `N` | `l_IDC` (mm) | f₀ measured (GHz) | λ₀/a |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ELC0 (plain gap) | 2 | 3.6 | **3.14** | 6.8 |
| ELC1b | 5 | 1.2 | 2.64 | 8.1 |
| ELC1a | 4 | 2.0 | 2.48 | 8.7 |
| ELC2b | 5 | 2.8 | 2.24 | 9.6 |
| ELC2a | 6 | 2.0 | **2.10** | 10.2 |

**A measured 2.10 → 3.14 GHz range — 1.50× — at an outer footprint and cell size held exactly constant.** Simulation and measurement agree to within 0.1 GHz on every sample.

Their design law is closed-form (their Eq. 5), for a fixed inductive loop:

```
f₀,new  =  sqrt( l₀ / ( l_IDC · (N − 1) ) )  ·  f₀
```

Two properties make this an unusually good fit for #130's symbol model. The lever is **strong** — a factor of 1.5 against the 1.61 that a 16× gap sweep buys, with far less demand on the printer. And `N` is an **integer**, so the alphabet is quantised by construction rather than by a downstream decision, which is what #130 asked for ("characterise on a continuous parameter, admit only the quantised set") and gets here for free.

### 4.3 What it does *not* remove — the honest counterweight

**Withayachumnankul, Fumeaux & Abbott, "Effects of mutual coupling in dual-resonance metamaterials", [arXiv:1109.0055](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.0055) (2011).** Retrieved in full.

This is the cleanest control experiment available for the whole interior-tuning idea, because it goes further than fixed outlines: **the geometry is not merely fixed, it is identical.** A 20 × 20 array of ELC resonators (cell `a` = 13 mm, footprint `d` = 11 mm, so a 2 mm gap everywhere) on FR4, each with a varactor at its central gap. Alternate rows are biased differently, so half the resonators are tuned to a different frequency **with no change of shape whatsoever**. Measured in an anechoic chamber against a VNA, simulated in HFSS, and fitted to a circuit model.

The result is not "no error":

> "it is found that the two resonances experience significant shifting and weakening as they become spectrally close."

Reading their Fig. 3 (simulated resonance frequency against bias, **INFERRED** from the plotted curves): the 0 V population resonates at **2.70 GHz** when all its neighbours are also at 0 V, and at **2.885 GHz** when its neighbours are tuned away to 24 V. That is a **+6.9% shift caused purely by the neighbours being different**. The 24 V population shifts +2.8% the other way (3.57 → 3.67 GHz).

The mechanism is inductive, not capacitive, which is exactly why holding the gap fixed does not kill it. Their fitted circuit gives a mutual inductance **M = 2.8 nH against a self-inductance L = 36.5 nH — a coupling of 7.7%** — and:

> "At M = 0, where the two systems are decoupled, the two resonances become comparable in strength. Hence, a difference in the resonance strengths is responsible purely by the inter-cell inductive coupling."

Note their electrical pitch: `a` = 13 mm at 2.7–3.6 GHz is **0.117–0.156 λ**, closely comparable to Example 3's `a₁` = 0.140 λ. This is the nearest analogue in the retrieved literature to Example 3's tight axis.

**How much phase error 6.9% of frequency pulling represents cannot be computed here** — it needs the element's reflection-phase-against-frequency curve, which needs a solve. One bounding observation, clearly marked as such: Landy et al. report their absorber's **FWHM as 4%** of centre frequency. If a comparable ERR alphabet carried comparable pulling, the shift would exceed the linewidth, and a resonance moved by more than its own width can move reflection phase by most of its full range. That is a reason to run the solve, **not** a result — Landy's 4% is a two-layer absorbance width and the 6.9% is a single-layer transmissive resonance pull, and they are not the same quantity.

---

## 5. Does the sizing rule survive a 4.2 × 12 mm cell?

`docs/supercell-sizing-rule.md` assumes a **square** cell at 0.4–0.5 λ. Example 3's is **4.2 × 12 mm = 0.140 λ × 0.400 λ at 10 GHz**: rectangular, with an aspect ratio of 2.86, and *far* more sub-wavelength on one axis than the rule contemplates. It does not survive unamended. Four amendments follow; the arithmetic is **CALCULATED**.

Throughout, the budget is the corrected, cancellation-derived one — not the ±22.5° quantisation half-step, which `docs/RUNNING-LISTS.md` §3 item 13 already flags as a beam-forming convention wrongly carried into a backscatter problem:

```
RCS reduction (dB) = −20 · log₁₀( sin(d/2) )        d = phase error from the ideal 180°
phase budget d     =  2 · arcsin( 10^(−RCSR_dB/20) )
```

| Required RCS reduction | 6 dB | 10 dB | 15 dB | 20 dB | 30 dB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase budget `d` | 60.2° | **36.9°** | 20.5° | 11.5° | 3.6° |

**The 10 dB figure is confirmed at primary level.** Haji-Ahmadi, Nayyeri, Soleimani & Ramahi, *Sci. Rep.* **7**:11437 (2017), retrieved via [PMC5595835](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595835/), state: *"It is theoretically proven that a phase difference of 180 ± 37° between the reflections from two region provides at least 10 dB monostatic RCS reduction"*, and use ±37° as their own optimisation criterion throughout. The formula above returns **36.87°** for 10 dB — agreement to 0.13°. Two independent routes to the same number. (Haji-Ahmadi attribute it to Chen, Balanis & Birtcher, *IEEE T-AP* **63**:2636–2645 (2015); that paper is **STRANDED** — OpenAlex confirms `oa_status: closed`, no repository copy. The criterion is nonetheless verified, because a retrieved paper states it and the physics reproduces it.)

### Amendment 1 — the boundary fraction needs two indices

For a block of `N_x × N_y` cells, the fraction of cells having at least one foreign neighbour is

```
f(N_x, N_y)  =  1 − (N_x − 2)(N_y − 2) / (N_x · N_y)      for N_x, N_y ≥ 2
             =  1                                          if either is 1
```

This reduces exactly to the document's `(4N−4)/N²` when `N_x = N_y` (checked for N = 2…10), so it is a generalisation, not a replacement.

### Amendment 2 — the scattering ceiling needs two block sizes, and the lobe is not on the diagonal

For blocks of side `a_x = N_x·p_x` and `a_y = N_y·p_y`, the chessboard's dominant spatial harmonic sits at `(k_x, k_y) = (±π/a_x, ±π/a_y)`, so

```
sin θ  =  (λ/2) · sqrt( 1/a_x² + 1/a_y² )          tan φ  =  a_x / a_y
```

which again reduces to the document's `λ/(a√2)` when `a_x = a_y`. The azimuth term is new and it is not cosmetic: with `a_x/a_y` = 4.2/12, a 1 × 1 block would throw its lobes at **φ = 19.3° from the long axis, not 45°**. Anyone measuring a coupon needs to know where to point the receiving horn.

### Amendment 3 — N = 2 is not available on this cell, and small blocks are forbidden

This is the substantive change. Requiring `sin θ ≤ 1` for the lobe to propagate at all:

| Block along `a₂` | Smallest block along `a₁` that radiates | Block size | θ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `N_y` = 2 | `N_x` = **5** | 21.0 × 24.0 mm = 0.70 × 0.80 λ | 71.5° |
| `N_y` = 3 | `N_x` = **4** | 16.8 × 36.0 mm = 0.56 × 1.20 λ | 79.9° |
| `N_y` ≥ 4 | `N_x` = **4** | — | 66–71° |

**Every block smaller than 5 × 2 cells is evanescent — it redirects nothing.** In the limit of a tall block the condition becomes simply `a_x ≥ λ/2` = 14.99 mm = **3.57 cells**: a coding block must be at least half a wavelength across on the coding axis, however small the cell is. The square-cell case hides this because at `p` = 0.5 λ the requirement `a ≥ λ/√2` is already met by `N` = 2.

The consequence runs the opposite way to the document's conclusion. Because blocks of 4–5 cells and up are *forced* by the physics, **`f(N)` is no longer pinned at 1 and the block genuinely averages.** The rule's central claim — "N = 2 is the only size allowed, so grouping averages nothing" — is a property of a half-wavelength square cell, not a general truth about coding metasurfaces.

### Amendment 4 — the block must fit on the panel, at least twice per axis

The document does not state this and it turns out to be the binding constraint on a coupon. A chessboard needs at least one full period per axis: `2·N_x·p_x ≤ L` and `2·N_y·p_y ≤ L`. On the 180 mm (6 λ) coupon [#106](https://github.com/parthalon025/Principle_RF_Engineer_Agent/issues/106) specifies, that caps `N_y` at 7 — and `N_y` = 7 already means a 84 mm block.

### The resulting feasibility table

Smallest feasible block for Example 3's cell at 10 GHz, given an alphabet's worst-case unlike-neighbour phase error `Δφ_max` and a required RCS reduction. `θ_min` is the panel's own specular half-width `λ/(2L)` — **4.78° for a 6 λ coupon, 0.95° for a 30 λ panel**.

| `Δφ_max` | 10 dB (budget 36.9°) | 15 dB (20.5°) | 20 dB (11.5°) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12° (fixed-edge / interior-tuned) | 5 × 2 → θ 71.5° | 5 × 2 → θ 71.5° | 4 × 3 → θ 79.9° |
| 20° | 5 × 2 → θ 71.5° | 5 × 2 → θ 71.5° | 7 × 5 → θ 34.6° |
| 25° (square patch @ 0.5 λ) | 5 × 2 → θ 71.5° | 5 × 3 → θ 55.7° | 9 × 7 → θ 25.8° |
| 45° (Minkowski @ 0.4 λ) | 5 × 3 → θ 55.7° | 9 × 7 → θ 25.8° | coupon: **none** · 30 λ panel: 17 × 13 → θ 13.3° |
| 85° (square patch @ 0.4 λ) | 10 × 7 → θ 23.5° | coupon: **none** · 30 λ: 18 × 14 → θ 12.6° | coupon: **none** · 30 λ: 32 × 26 → θ 7.0° |

**At 10 dB, every alphabet in the literature has a feasible block on this cell, even on a coupon.** The gate only starts biting at 15 dB and above, and what it bites is the *coupon*, not the design.

### One disagreement with the corrected rule as stated to me

The coordinator's note says *"at 20 dB the square patch at 0.4 λ has no feasible N at all."* Running the same constraints on a **square** 0.4 λ cell, I get:

| Square cell, p = 0.4 λ | 6 λ coupon | 30 λ panel |
|---|---|---|
| Square patch, `Δφ_max` = 85° | **none at 10, 15 or 20 dB** | 10 × 7 (10 dB) · 18 × 14 (15 dB) · **32 × 26 (20 dB, θ = 3.6°)** |
| Minkowski, 45° | 5 × 3 at 10 dB only | 5 × 3 · 9 × 7 · 17 × 13 |
| Fixed-edge, 20° | 2 × 2 · 2 × 2 · 7 × 5 | 2 × 2 · 2 × 2 · 7 × 5 |

So the statement is **true on a coupon and false on a large panel** — on 30 λ the square patch has a feasible block at 20 dB (32 × 26 cells, θ = 3.6°, comfortably above the 0.95° specular half-width). And on the coupon it has none *even at 10 dB*, which is stronger than stated. The reason in both directions is Amendment 4: the block must fit twice. This reinforces the coordinator's own counterintuitive point — the coupon is the hard case — but relocates the mechanism from the scattering angle to the panel-fit constraint. A 32 × 26 block of 0.4 λ cells is also a place where the "infinite periodic chessboard" assumption is under real strain, so I would not lean on that entry hard.

---

## 6. If the outline has to stay put: the fixed-outline variant

The equivalent of the fixed-edge Minkowski cell, for this family, exists and is measured. It is §4.2's **interdigital-capacitor-loaded ELC**. In plain terms: instead of making the shape bigger or smaller, you leave its outline exactly where it is and **re-cut the small break inside it into interleaved fingers, like two combs pushed together.** More fingers means more capacitance, which means a lower resonant frequency, and nothing outside the element has moved.

Why it fits this project specifically:

- **Measured, not simulated** — 1.50× frequency range across five letters, and #130 already notes a per-letter measured library has no prior art. This is the closest thing to one.
- **Zero gap excursion by construction** — the neighbour never sees a different edge.
- **Naturally quantised** — the finger count `N` is an integer.
- **Printable** — the authors note *"the feature size of an IDC does not need to be finer than the gap width of an ordinary ELC resonator"*. Theirs is `w = g = 0.4 mm`; Example 3's tightest existing feature is 0.6 mm and the NOVA's floor is 0.1 mm, so this adds no new process demand.

**The honest gap in this recommendation.** Withayachumnankul's ELC has **one gap, in the centre**; Landy's ERR has **two gaps, in the side arms**. Transferring the trick means either putting interdigital fingers into Example 3's two `G` gaps, or adopting a centre-gap ELC in place of the I-shape. Both are plausible — the capacitance is a lumped element in either topology — but **neither is published for Landy's geometry**, and Eq. (5)'s assumption that "the inductance loop remains unchanged" would need checking for a two-gap ring. That is a solve, not a search.

A second, cheaper option deserves recording: **Landy's own out-of-plane knob, the spacer `h`.** It touches no gap at all. It cannot vary letter to letter on one printed sheet — but it is the right lever for moving the *whole* design's band, and #104 already records it as the thing to sweep.

---

## 7. Honest limits

- **No phase error is computed here, and none could be.** `Δφ_max` for an I-shape alphabet needs the extended-local-periodicity solve #138 itself defers — the element with eight identical neighbours, then with two swapped. Everything in §3 is a *gap* excursion, which is the input to that error, not the error. §5's feasibility table is therefore parameterised by `Δφ_max`, not evaluated at one.
- **Which plane dominates is unresolved, and it is the crux.** Costanzo's "E-plane is worse" is established for variable-size microstrip patches, where the radiating edges face along the E-plane. Example 3's tight 0.2 mm ERR gap is on the **H**-plane, and its tight 0.2 mm cut-wire gap is on the **E**-plane, one layer down. Assuming Costanzo's anisotropy carries over to a two-layer ERR-and-wire cell is **INFERRED and may well be wrong**. The extended-local-periodicity protocol must be run **on both axes** for this cell and the worse taken — that is Amendment 3's practical corollary and it doubles the solve count.
- **`f₀ ∝ 1/size` is a first-order scaling.** §3's dimension ranges assume it. Real ELC and cut-wire resonances depart from it, more so as the element becomes a large fraction of the cell — which, at `W`/`a₁` = 0.95, it already is. The *gap ratios* are less sensitive to this than the dimension ranges, but they are not immune.
- **The ERR's height is measured off a drawing, not published.** 3.96 mm from Landy's Fig. 1(a) at 0.05% scale agreement; ≈3.8–4.0 mm from the patent's FIG. 7E. Neither dimension table names it. Every `a₂`-axis ERR gap figure (8.0 mm, 0.267 λ) inherits that.
- **The 6.9% pulling in §4.3 is read off a plotted curve**, is *simulated* rather than measured (their Fig. 3 is the HFSS series; the measurement is the transmission spectra of Fig. 2), and is for a single-layer transmissive ELC panel at 3 GHz, not a ground-backed X-band absorber. It is the right order of magnitude and the wrong structure.
- **Frequency ambiguity.** The patent's FIG. 7G puts the absorption peak at ≈9.2 GHz (`INFERRED` from the plot, per #116). Landy et al. measured this same geometry peaking at **11.5 GHz**, simulating 11.65 GHz. λ-normalised figures are given at 10 GHz throughout for consistency with #104; at 11.5 GHz the pitches become 0.161 λ and 0.460 λ and the gaps 0.0077 λ. **The discrepancy is not explained here** and is worth a ticket of its own — it may be the difference between Landy's FR4/adhesive/FR4 sandwich and the patent's assumption of solid FR4 at εr = 4.8 across the full 0.72 mm.
- **Example 3 itself does not need any of this.** It is a Tier A uniform surface: every cell is identical, there are no unlike neighbours, and the coupling error is zero by construction. This document is about whether the *shape* is a good candidate letter for a Tier B alphabet.

**What would falsify this.** A solve — or a measurement — showing that an I-shape alphabet tuned purely on `G` (or on interdigital finger count) still exceeds the phase budget at 4.2 mm pitch. That would mean the residual inductive channel of §4.3 dominates, interior tuning is not the lever it appears to be for *this* cell, and the answer is to open the pitch rather than to redesign the letter. The converse test is cheaper and should come first: run Costanzo's protocol on both cell axes and see whether the H-plane 0.2 mm gap or the E-plane 8.0 mm gap sets `Δφ_max`. If it is the H-plane, everything above holds. If it is the E-plane, the cut wire is the problem and the ERR was never the question.
